quick: Refraction: 1-2 drops, repeat at 5-10 min intervals as needed; uveitis: 1-2 drops 2-3 times daily
Use only if clearly needed; minimal systemic exposure
Caution; minimal systemic absorption with topical use
Intraocular pressure, signs of angle closure, systemic anticholinergic effects in children
summary: Homatropine hydrobromide is a topical ophthalmic antimuscarinic that produces moderately long-acting mydriasis (pupil dilation) and cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation). It is used for cycloplegic refraction, to treat inflammatory conditions of the uveal tract (e.g., uveitis/iritis), and to manage pre- and postoperative states requiring mydriasis. By blocking muscarinic receptors of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, it dilates the pupil and relaxes the ciliary muscle. It can precipitate angle-closure glaucoma in predisposed eyes and cause systemic anticholinergic effects, especially in children.
indications: Treatment of inflammatory conditions of the uveal tract (e.g., uveitis, iritis)
Pre- and postoperative states when mydriasis is required
Optical aid in some cases of axial lens opacities

dosage.d: 1-2 drops of 2% or 5% solution, repeat every 5-10 minutes

dosage.n: Up to every 3-4 hours in severe cases

dosage.d: 1 drop of lower concentration, repeat once in 10 min if needed
dosage.n: Use lowest concentration; watch for systemic effects

admin: Instill into the conjunctival sac; do not touch the dropper tip to the eye
Apply gentle pressure on the inner corner (nasolacrimal occlusion) for 1-2 minutes to reduce systemic absorption
Wipe away excess solution from around the eye
Use the lowest effective concentration, especially in children and the elderly
Wash hands before and after use
moa: Homatropine is a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. In the eye it blocks the responses of the sphincter muscle of the iris and the ciliary muscle to cholinergic stimulation, producing pupillary dilation (mydriasis) and paralysis of accommodation (cycloplegia). It is less potent and shorter-acting than atropine.

absolute: Primary (narrow-angle) glaucoma or anatomically narrow angles
Known hypersensitivity to homatropine or other belladonna alkaloids
relative: Infants and small children (greater susceptibility to systemic anticholinergic toxicity)
Elderly or others at risk of undiagnosed angle-closure glaucoma
monitor: Intraocular pressure and signs of acute angle closure (eye pain, redness, halos)
Systemic anticholinergic effects, especially in children (flushing, fever, tachycardia)

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies. With topical ocular use systemic exposure is low; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: It is not known to what extent homatropine is excreted in human milk after ophthalmic use; systemic absorption is minimal. Use with caution and consider nasolacrimal occlusion to limit absorption.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required; systemic absorption from ophthalmic use is minimal.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is required; systemic absorption from ophthalmic use is minimal.

moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs (systemic atropine-like agents) - additive antimuscarinic effects if systemic absorption occurs
Pilocarpine and other miotics (opposing pharmacologic effect)
minor: Carbachol and cholinesterase inhibitors (antagonistic ocular effects)
interactions.diagnostics: Causes pupil dilation that may interfere with subsequent fundus/IOP examination timing

common: Transient stinging or burning on instillation
serious: Systemic anticholinergic toxicity (tachycardia, dry mouth, flushing, fever, hallucinations) - especially in children
rare: Psychotic reactions and behavioral disturbances (mainly pediatric)
Vasodilation / cardiovascular effects with significant systemic absorption
emergency: Severe systemic anticholinergic toxicity (hyperthermia, delirium, tachyarrhythmia) in children

monitoring: Intraocular pressure in patients at risk of glaucoma
Systemic anticholinergic signs, especially in infants and children
Resolution of ocular inflammation when used for uveitis
counsel: Your vision will be blurry and you will be sensitive to light for several hours to days - wear sunglasses
Do not drive or operate machinery until vision clears
Press gently on the inner corner of the eye for a minute after putting in drops to reduce body-wide effects
Seek urgent care for severe eye pain, sudden vision loss, or halos around lights
In children, report flushing, fever, fast heartbeat, or unusual behavior
Do not let the dropper tip touch the eye or any surface
pk: Mydriasis and cycloplegia begin within 10-30 minutes of instillation
Topical ocular effect-based; systemic kinetics minimal with proper use
Mydriasis and cycloplegia typically last 1-3 days
Store at controlled room temperature 15-30 C; keep tightly closed and protect from light
pearls: Moderately long-acting mydriatic/cycloplegic - intermediate between tropicamide and atropine
Nasolacrimal occlusion after instillation limits systemic anticholinergic absorption
Contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma - can precipitate an acute attack
Children are especially prone to systemic anticholinergic toxicity - use the lowest concentration
Used in uveitis to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent posterior synechiae
missed: If a scheduled dose is missed (e.g., for uveitis), instill it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule - do not double up.
overdose: Systemic overdose (from excessive instillation or ingestion) produces anticholinergic toxicity: flushing, dry warm skin, fever, dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention, restlessness, hallucinations, and in severe cases coma and circulatory collapse. Treatment is supportive; physostigmine can reverse severe central and cardiovascular anticholinergic effects, with management of hyperthermia.
